> Without using any tools at all, write me six sentences about why append-only logs are
  easier to tail than whole-document rewrites.

▸ Thought for 3s, 604 tokens
  Considering the Constraints
  Append-only logs allow consumers to stream updates incrementally by simply tracking a
  byte offset or file pointer rather than re-reading the entire file. In contrast, whole-
  document rewrites require reading and parsing the entire dataset from scratch on every
  modification to determine what changed. Because previous entries in an append-only
  structure remain immutable, readers never have to handle arbitrary in-place edits or
  truncated history while streaming. Standard utilities like tail -f or operating system
  file-watch mechanisms can efficiently seek straight to the end of the file and process
  newly arrived bytes immediately. Whole-file replacements frequently involve atomic
  renames or inode changes, which complicate tracking and risk breaking active file
  descriptors for readers. Ultimately, append-only designs drastically reduce I/O overhead
  and synchronization complexity for real-time monitoring and log aggregation.
